Decompose the figure into the central 3×3 square and four attached triangles. The square has area 3×3=9.
Each triangle has base 2 and height 1, so its area is 2×1/2=1. The total area is 9+4×1=13.
The one-unit border uses 12×16-10×14=192-140=52 small tiles. Subtracting the inner rectangle avoids double-counting the corners.
The interior area is 10×14=140, filled with tiles of area 2×2=4, requiring 140/4=35 tiles. The total count is 52+35=87.
Decompose the figure along the unit grid. It contains four full squares and twelve triangles, each occupying half a square.
The total area is 4+12×(1/2)=4+6=10 square inches.
The shaded region can be counted as two differences of square areas. The first contributes 10^{2}-9^{2}=100-81=19.
The second contributes 7^{2}-4^{2}=49-16=33. Adding the two shaded contributions gives 19+33=52.
Count the star as four complete unit squares and eight half-squares. Its area is 4+8/2=8 square units.
The entire grid has area 16 square units. Thus the star covers 8/16=1/2 of the grid, which is 50%.
Each rectangle has area 5×3=15. In their rotated positions, the overlap is a square of side 5/2=2.5, which fits within the other dimension 3.
Add the two rectangle areas and subtract the overlap counted twice: 15+15-2.5^{2}=30-6.25=23.75.
The unreachable interior is a rectangle measuring 10-2=8 by 8-2=6. Its area is 8×6=48.
The entire rectangle has area 10×8=80, so the reachable border has area 80-48=32. The required fraction is 32/80=2/5.

answer.value: Equal areas; figure I has the smaller perimeter
steps: Take one grid spacing as one unit. Figure I has area 1. Splitting figure II along the horizontal grid line gives two triangles of area 1/2 each, so its area is also 1.
Find the slanted boundary lengths with the Pythagorean theorem. Figure I has perimeter 2+2√2.
Figure II has perimeter 1+2√2+√5. Subtracting the first perimeter from the second gives √5−1.
Since √5>1, this difference is positive. The figures have equal areas, but figure I has the smaller perimeter.
Complete the region by adding a rectangle beneath BD. Its width is 10 and its height is 5, so its area is 50.
The curved part above the rectangle includes a semicircle of area 25π/2.
The two removed quarter-circles together also have area 25π/2, because their combined fraction of a full circle is one half.
These curved areas cancel exactly: required area=25π/2+50−25π/2=50. Thus the answer comes entirely from the added rectangle; no decimal approximation to π is needed.
Use the grid to divide each candidate into complete unit squares and half-squares. Keep the same unit of area for all five figures.
The resulting areas of A, B, and C are each 5 square units.
Figure D has area 4.5, while figure E has area 5.5.
Since 5.5 exceeds 5 and 4.5, figure E is the largest. Comparing actual area, rather than perimeter or the apparent width of a drawing, distinguishes the two close candidates.
Enclose the figure in a 10 by 10 rectangle of area 100, and subtract the regions outside the target.
The upper-left part can be split vertically into a trapezoid of width 3 with parallel sides 5 and 6, area 3(5+6)/2=16.5.
Beside it is a triangle with base 7 and height 6, area 21. The two other outside triangles have areas 30 and 10.
Thus the target area is 100−16.5−21−30−10=22.5.
Complete the shape to an 8 by 9 rectangle with area 72. The original area is 52, so the missing rectangle has area 72−52=20.
Its height is DE=9−5=4.
Dividing area by height gives its width EF=20÷4=5.
Thus DE+EF=4+5=9. The missing area is useful because the notch is rectangular; it converts an irregular outline into two directly related side lengths.
Join the center of the regular hexagon to all six vertices. This splits it into six congruent equilateral triangles.
Each has side length 1, because a regular hexagon's center-to-vertex radius equals its side length.
The six exterior triangles are congruent to these six interior triangles.
Thus the hexagon and the total exterior region each consist of six copies of the same triangle. Their area ratio is 6:6=1:1, without needing the equilateral-triangle area formula.
The full region has area 10, so the lower half must have area 5. The unit square on the right contributes area 1.
The remaining triangular part must therefore have area 5−1 = 4. Its base is 5, so its height h satisfies 5h/2 = 4, giving h = 8/5.
The marked lengths are QY = h−1 = 3/5 and XQ = 2−h = 2/5. Their ratio is XQ/QY = (2/5)/(3/5) = 2/3.
The two square areas add to 450, but their union, the large rectangle, has area 375. The excess comes from counting the overlap twice.
Therefore the overlap area is 450−375 = 75. This is the inclusion-exclusion relation: sum of areas equals union area plus overlap area.
The requested percentage uses the large rectangle as the whole, so divide by 375: 75/375 = 1/5 = 20%. Dividing by 450 would use a total that counts the overlap twice.
Each of the ten smaller squares has a positive integer side length, so each has area at least 1. The enclosing square therefore has area at least 10.
Its side length is an integer, so it cannot be 3 or smaller: a 3×3 square has area only 9. This proves a lower bound of 4 for its side.
To attain it, divide a 4×4 square into two 2×2 squares across the upper half and eight 1×1 squares across the lower half. This uses exactly 10 squares.
The portions of the three circles inside the rectangle are quarter-circles, with radii 1, 2, and 3. They do not overlap in the rectangle.
Their combined area is π(1^{2}+2^{2}+3^{2})/4 = 14π/4 = 3.5π.

Subtract this from the rectangle's area 15 to get the remaining area 15−3.5π. Numerically this is approximately 4.004, so the closest listed estimate is 4.0. Adding the sector areas is valid because their interiors are disjoint.
Enclose the triangle in the rectangle from x = 1 to x = 5 and y = 1 to y = 4. This rectangle has width 4, height 3, and area 12.
The three parts outside the triangle but inside that rectangle are right triangles. Their areas are 4×2/2 = 4, 3×1/2 = 1.5, and 1×3/2 = 1.5.
Subtracting gives the target triangle's area as 12−4−1.5−1.5 = 5. The full grid has area 30, so the desired fraction is 5/30 = 1/6.
Compare the three right triangles outside the target region with the surrounding rectangle. Their base and height fractions determine their area fractions.
Using area=base×height÷2, the three outside pieces occupy 1/4, 1/4, and 1/8 of the rectangle respectively.
Their combined fraction is 1/4+1/4+1/8=5/8. Thus the central target region occupies the remaining 1−5/8=3/8.
The rectangle's area is 72 square units, so the requested area is 72×3/8=27.

This subtraction method uses all the complementary pieces exactly once. It also shows that the answer depends on area fractions, so calculating the lengths of the target region's slanted sides is unnecessary.
Choose a 6 by 6 repeating square from the pattern. Its total area is 36 square units, and the repeating proportions make it sufficient to examine this one square.
The dark central square measures 2 by 2, contributing area 4.
Four dark rectangles each measure 2 by 1, contributing another 8.
Four dark triangles each have base 2 and height 1, contributing 4×(2×1/2)=4.

These nonoverlapping pieces give dark area 4+8+4=16. The dark fraction is therefore 16/36=4/9. Using one complete repeating unit avoids giving the boundary pieces too much or too little weight in the overall proportion.
The enclosing rectangle has area 10×8=80. The four triangles outside the parallelogram have areas 6, 15, 6, and 15.
Their combined area is 42, so the parallelogram has area 80−42=38.
Side HE is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 3 and 4, hence HE=√(3^{2}+4^{2})=5.
Use HE as the base of the parallelogram. Since area=base×perpendicular height, the required height is 38÷5=7.6.
This uses a perpendicular height to HE, not the rectangle's vertical height. Computing the parallelogram's area first avoids needing to find a new angle or a slanted distance directly.
The two squares have combined separate area 32. Their overlap is a square of side 2, with area 4.
Subtract the overlap once to find their union: 32−4=28.
The circle's diameter is the diagonal of that overlap square. By the Pythagorean theorem, the diameter is 2√2, so the radius is √2.
Its area is therefore π(√2)^{2}=2π.

The shaded area is the union of the squares with this circle removed, giving 28−2π. Subtracting the overlap twice would remove a region that belongs in the union, while using side 2 as the circle's diameter would misread the diagonal in the diagram.
Separate the diagram into the region common to the circle and square and their two nonoverlapping parts.
The given equality concerns those two nonoverlapping areas. Add the common area to both sides of that equality.
This shows that the entire circle and the entire square have equal area.
The square has area 4, so πr^{2}=4. Dividing by π gives r^{2}=4/π, and taking the positive square root gives r=2/√π.
This argument avoids calculating any individual curved segment. Adding the same shared area preserves the equality, while the positive root is required because r is a geometric length.
Use the center and the inner concave vertices to split each wing into two triangles.
For each small triangle, the base is 1 and the perpendicular height is 1.5, so its area is 1×1.5/2=0.75.
Two such triangles make one complete wing, with area 2×0.75=1.5.
There are four congruent wings, and they do not overlap except along their boundaries.

The total area is therefore 4×1.5=6 square units. The partition is useful because the visible wings have slanted edges, but every triangular piece has a simple base and perpendicular height. Count all eight small triangles once rather than estimating the area from the overall outline.
Scale the square to side length 3; scaling does not affect the requested area ratio.
The given divisions then give AF=CD=2 and EF=ED=1. Use the complementary regions rather than trying to find the target polygon's slanted sides.
The three outside right triangles have areas 3, 3, and 1/2 respectively.
The square has area 9, so the target area is 9−3−3−1/2=5/2.
Its fraction of the square is (5/2)/9=5/18. The subtraction includes each outside triangle once, and the final division by 9 converts the computed area back into the required ratio.
The outer square has area 4. The inner square can be partitioned into four right triangles with perpendicular legs 1, each of area 1×1/2 = 1/2.
Thus the inner square has area 4×(1/2) = 2. The circle has area π, so the shaded part inside the circle but outside the inner square has area π−2.
The region between the two squares has area 4−2 = 2. The ratio of the two indicated areas is therefore (π−2)/2.
This is approximately 0.571. Comparing with the answer choices, the nearest listed value is 1/2; the exact ratio itself is (π−2)/2.
Enclose the star-shaped region in a square of side length 4. The square's area is 4^{2} = 16.
The portions outside the star but inside the square are four quarter-circles of radius 2. Their total area equals one full circle of radius 2: π×2^{2} = 4π.
The star's area is therefore 16−4π. The original circle also has radius 2 and area 4π.
Divide the star's area by the original circle's area: (16−4π)/(4π) = (4−π)/π. This subtraction uses the square as a convenient common enclosure.
The four corner right triangles are congruent. Denote their perpendicular legs by a and b, so each has area ab/2.
Together they occupy exactly the area between the two squares. The difference of the square areas is 5−4 = 1.
Thus 4×ab/2 = 1, or 2ab = 1. Dividing by 2 gives ab = 1/2.
The individual lengths a and b need not be found: the area difference determines their product directly. Congruence ensures that all four triangles contribute the same area.
Take each square's side length to be 1. This rescales every area by the same factor, so it leaves the desired fraction unchanged.
Extend IJ upward to a point K for which AK is horizontal. The completed right triangle AKJ has legs AK = 1.5 and KJ = 2.
Its area is 1.5×2/2 = 1.5. The part added outside the desired shaded region is the upper-right rectangle, with width 0.5 and height 1, so its area is 0.5.
The shaded area is consequently 1.5−0.5 = 1. The three unit squares have total area 3, giving shaded fraction 1/3.
Each mountain is an isosceles right triangle with 45° base angles. If its height is t, its base is 2t, so its area is (1/2)(2t)t=t^{2}.
The two full triangle areas therefore sum to 8^{2}+12^{2}=64+144=208.

Their overlap is a similar isosceles right triangle. If its height is h, its area is h^{2}. Since the union has area 183, inclusion-exclusion gives 208-h^{2}=183. Adding the two mountain areas counts every overlapped point twice, so the overlap must be subtracted exactly once to obtain their union.
Thus h^{2}=25. Height is positive, so h=5.
The small rectangular sheet has area 6×7=42, while its kite has area 21. The unused area is therefore 42−21=21.
Both dimensions are multiplied by 3, so areas are multiplied by 3^{2}=9. The unused area becomes 21×9=189 square units.
The two midlines divide the large square into eight congruent small right triangles.
The central square consists of four of these eight triangles, so it occupies 4/8=1/2 of the large square. Half of the given total area is 30, which is the required area.
Use a small grid square as one area unit. The central square has side length 2, so its area is 4; two side pieces add one unit each, giving shaded area 6.
The full 4 by 4 square has area 16, leaving unshaded area 10. The ratio is 6:10=3:5.
Express each shaded region as a fraction of one large square. The four contributions are 1/4, 1/8, 3/8, and 1/4.
Their sum is 2/8+1/8+3/8+2/8 = 1 whole square. Relative to four squares altogether, the shaded fraction is 1/4 = 25%.
Join O to all eight vertices. This divides the octagon into eight triangles of equal area.
The shaded region contains three whole wedges in the BCDE portion plus the half-wedge OBX. Thus it occupies 3+1/2 = 3.5 of the eight equal parts, or 3.5/8 = 7/16.
The large triangle on the left has area 4 square units. The smaller unshaded triangle at its top left is similar to that large triangle.
Its corresponding lengths are half as large. Areas scale by the square of the length factor, so its area is (1/2)^{2}×4=1.
The shaded part is the large left triangle with this small triangle removed.
Therefore its area is 4−1=3. Using a factor of 1/2 for the area would be incorrect; the scale factor must be squared.
The two equal small circles have total area 1, so each has area 1/2. From the configuration, the large circle's radius is twice a small circle's radius.
Circle area scales with the square of the radius. Thus the large circle has four times a small circle's area: 4×(1/2)=2.
The shaded region is the large circle minus the two small circles. Its area is therefore 2-1=1. The factor π cancels in the area comparison.
Joining the four side midpoints produces a parallelogram. From the coordinates, its base is 2-(-3)=5 and its perpendicular height is 4.
Its area is therefore 5×4=20. The four corner triangles outside this midpoint parallelogram together occupy half of the original rectangle.
Consequently the midpoint parallelogram also has half the rectangle's area. Doubling gives the original rectangle area 2×20=40.
The large and small equilateral triangles have side-length ratio 3:2, so their areas are in ratio 3^{2}:2^{2}=9:4.
Use area units in which the large triangle has area 9 and the inner triangle area 4. The three equal trapezoids together have area 9-4=5.
Each trapezoid therefore has area 5/3. Its area relative to the inner triangle is (5/3):4. Multiply both terms by 3 to obtain 5:12.

The entire gap between the left circle and its inscribed square is shaded, but only one quarter of the corresponding right gap is shaded. Equal shaded areas mean the full right gap is four times the left gap.
The two circle-and-square configurations are similar. Since the left radius is 1 and the right radius is R, their linear scale factor is R, so all areas scale by R^{2}.
Therefore R^{2}=4. Taking the positive root gives R=2 units.
The regular hexagon can be divided by joining its center to its vertices. This creates six congruent equilateral triangles.
Each small equilateral triangle has side length half that of the original equilateral triangle. Areas of similar figures scale as the square of the side-length ratio.
Since the original triangle has area 4, each small triangle has area 4×(1/2)^{2} = 1.
The six small triangles exactly fill the hexagon, so its area is 6×1 = 6. Using the squared scale factor is necessary; halving a side quarters the area.
The area of triangle ABD is one third of the full area 360, hence 120. Because E is the midpoint of BD, triangles ABE and AED have equal bases and the same altitude from A. Thus ABE has area 60.
Relative to BC, D has two thirds of A's height. Since E is halfway from B to D, E has one third of A's height.
Along AF this means AE:EF=2:1.
Triangles ABE and EBF have bases AE and EF on the same line and the same altitude from B, so their areas are also in ratio 2:1. Therefore EBF has area 60/2=30.
Let s be the side of a small shaded square and d the common gap width. Counting along one side of the large square gives its side length L=24s+25d.

The shaded area is 576s^{2}=(24s)^{2} and equals 64% of the large square's area. Thus (24s)^{2}=0.64L^{2}. The square roots use positive lengths: the area fraction 0.64 becomes the side-length fraction √0.64=0.8, rather than remaining 0.64.
Taking positive square roots gives 24s=0.8L, so L=30s. Substitute this into the length equation: 30s=24s+25d.
Therefore 25d=6s and d/s=6/25. This ratio also checks the stated side length: 24s+25(6s/25)=30s.

Areas of similar triangles are proportional to the squares of corresponding heights. Thus the relevant triangular areas can be compared using their squared heights with the common proportionality factor canceled.

The equality of the two shaded areas gives h^{2}-11^{2}=(h-5)^{2}. The left side represents the larger triangular area minus the height-11 triangle. Subtracting triangular areas is valid here because both smaller triangles use the same proportionality constant relating area to squared height.
Expand the right side: h^{2}-121=h^{2}-10h+25. Cancel h^{2} to obtain 10h=146.
Hence h=14.6. Checking, 14.6^{2}-121=92.16 and (14.6-5)^{2}=9.6^{2}=92.16, so the two areas do agree.
Compare the three radii. X has radius π. For Y, circumference 8π gives radius 8π/(2π)=4.
For Z, area 9π gives πr^{2}=9π, so r=3. Since 3<π<4, the increasing radius order is Z, X, Y.
Split the route into circular arcs and straight segments. The outer quarter-circle arc contributes length 10π.
The two inner quarter-circle arcs together contribute another 10π.
The straight parts consist of two radial gaps of length 10 and the inner diameter of length 20. Their combined length is 10+10+20=40.
Adding curved and straight parts gives 10π+10π+40=20π+40. Only the portions actually followed along the route are included; full circle circumferences would overcount the arcs.
Each curved segment is a quarter circle. The radii read from the construction are 1, 1, 2, 3, and 5.
A quarter circle of radius r has length (1/4)(2πr)=πr/2. Thus all five arc lengths can be added by first adding their radii.
The radius sum is 1+1+2+3+5=12. The total length is (π/2)×12=6π.
The ball has radius 2. Its center follows a path parallel to the track, but the radius of that path depends on whether the track curves inward or outward.
On the two concave sections, the ball's center is 2 units nearer the section's center, so the path radii are 100−2 = 98 and 80−2 = 78.
On the middle convex section, the center is 2 units farther away, giving path radius 60+2 = 62. Using the track radii themselves would therefore give the wrong distance.
Each section is a semicircle, whose arc length is π times its radius. The total distance traveled by the ball's center is π(98+62+78) = 238π.
For any semicircle of diameter d, the arc length is half the circumference: πd/2. Thus the arc length is always π/2 times its diameter.
The diameters of all the semicircular sections together span 1 mile. Adding their arc lengths therefore gives (π/2)×1 = π/2 miles, regardless of how the mile is divided into individual diameters.
At a constant speed of 5 miles per hour, time equals distance divided by speed.
The required time is (π/2)/5 = π/10 hour. This works by summing the diameters first, so the radius of each individual semicircle is unnecessary.

Separate the tight band into straight tangent segments and circular arcs. For equal-radius circles, each common external tangent segment has the same length as the corresponding segment between the centers.
The four straight lengths are 4, 4, 8, and 4. Their total is 20.

As the band travels once around the outside, its total turning is 360°. Therefore its curved pieces, all of radius 2, together have the length of one complete radius-2 circle. The tangent directions make one complete turn around the band. Each arc contributes its turning angle, so their angles sum to one full revolution.
That curved length is 2π×2=4π. Adding straight and curved portions gives 20+4π.
The large circle has diameter 12, hence radius 6. Six small-circle diameters fill the same width, so each small circle has diameter 2 and radius 1.
The 24 nonoverlapping small circles have total area 24π. The large circle's area is 36π, giving covered fraction 24π/(36π) = 2/3.
As the radius takes values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the circumference values are 2π, 4π, 6π, 8π, 10π. They are equally spaced horizontally.
The corresponding areas are π, 4π, 9π, 16π, 25π.
Their successive vertical increases are 3π, 5π, 7π, 9π, which grow rather than stay constant.
Thus the plotted points rise increasingly steeply, with equal horizontal gaps. Only graph A has this pattern; area is quadratic in radius, unlike circumference.
Let s be the square's side and r the circle's radius. Equal areas mean s^{2} = πr^{2}.
Divide by r^{2}, which is positive, to obtain (s/r)^{2} = π. Taking the positive square root gives s/r = √π.
Only the positive root is relevant because side lengths and radii are positive. The ratio therefore depends only on the area formulas, not on the common numerical area of the two figures.
The rectangle has side lengths AB = 30 and AD = 45, giving area 30×45 = 1350.
Each indicated semicircle has radius 15. Together the two semicircles have the same area as a full circle of radius 15, namely π×15^{2} = 225π.
The ratio of the rectangle's area to their combined area is 1350:225π. Divide both terms by 225 to simplify this to 6:π. Combining the semicircles first avoids carrying separate half-area factors.
Choose one grid interval as the length unit. The large enclosing circle has radius 3, the middle circle radius 2, each of the two white circles radius 1, and each small shaded circle radius 1/2.
Add shaded areas and subtract the white areas: π×2^{2}-2π×1^{2}+3π×(1/2)^{2}=π(4-2+3/4)=11π/4.
The enclosing circle has area 9π. Thus the shaded fraction is (11π/4)/(9π)=11/36.
The full circle has area 9π, so half its area is 9π/2=4.5π. This is the required shaded area.
The completely shaded inner annulus already contributes (2^{2}-1^{2})π=3π. The outer annulus must therefore contribute 4.5π-3π=1.5π.
The outer annulus has area (3^{2}-2^{2})π=5π. Its shaded fraction is 1.5π/(5π)=3/10, so the sector angle is 360°×3/10=108°.
Compare the shaded areas within equal 2 by 2 squares. For A, subtract the circle area π from the square area 4, giving 4−π.
In B, the four smaller circles have combined area 4×(π/4)=π. Its shaded area is therefore also 4−π.
For C, the circle has area π. The inner square has diagonal 2 and therefore area 2, giving shaded area π−2.
Compare π−2 with 4−π: their difference is 2π−6=2(π−3), which is positive because π>3.
Thus C alone has the greater shaded area. The comparison uses exact expressions rather than estimates from the appearance of the drawings.
Read the successive radii as 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12. The black regions are the central disk and the rings from radius 4 to 6 and from radius 8 to 10.
A ring's area is the outer disk area minus the inner disk area.
The full target is a disk of radius 12, with area 144π. Its black fraction is 60π/(144π)=5/12.
As a percentage, 5/12≈41.67%, nearest to 42%. Subtract the inner disk from each black ring; adding three whole disks would incorrectly include the white regions inside the outer rings.
From the figure, PQ and RS each have length 2. These are the diameters of the two smaller semicircles, so each has radius 1.
Each small semicircle has area π×1^{2}/2 = π/2. Together they have area π.
The large circle has radius √2, so its area is π(√2)^{2} = 2π.
Therefore the indicated area fraction is π/(2π) = 1/2. The π factors cancel, leaving a ratio determined by the squared radii and the two half-circle factors.
The two segments US and UT both have length 2 and form a 60° angle, so triangle UST is equilateral. Its area is (√3/4)×2^{2} = √3.
Each relevant arc has radius 2 and central angle 60°. Its chord therefore has length 2. In particular SR = TR = ST = 2, so triangle SRT is also equilateral with area √3.
The rhombus formed by these two triangles has area 2√3. Each curved piece to be removed is a circular segment: a 60° sector minus an equilateral triangle.
The sector area is (60/360)π×2^{2} = 2π/3, so each segment has area 2π/3−√3. Removing two such pieces gives 2√3−2(2π/3−√3) = 4√3−4π/3.
Consider a cross-section of the tape roll. The tape occupies an annulus with outer radius 2 and inner radius 1, so its area is π(2^{2}-1^{2})=3π square inches.
Unrolling the tape produces a long thin rectangle in the same cross-section. Its thickness is 0.015 inch; if the length is L, its area is 0.015L.

Area is conserved, so 0.015L=3π. Therefore L=3π/0.015=200π inches. The conversion from cross-sectional area to length works because every layer has the same thickness and the tape has no intervening gaps in this model.
Using π≈3.1416 gives L≈628.3 inches. The closest multiple of 100 inches is 600, since 628.3 is below the midpoint 650.
The radius CB is perpendicular to the tangent chord AD. A perpendicular from the outer circle's center to a chord bisects that chord, so AB = 8.
Let R and r be the outer and inner radii. The right triangle formed by the center, the midpoint B, and the chord endpoint A gives R^{2} = r^{2}+8^{2}.
Therefore R^{2}−r^{2} = 64. The annulus area is πR^{2}−πr^{2} = π(R^{2}−r^{2}) = 64π. The individual radii are unnecessary.
Place the origin at the center of the symmetric figure. The nearest inward corners are (±1,±2) and (±2,±1), all at distance √5 from the origin. A centered circle of radius √5 fits, giving area 5π.
To show that a larger circle cannot fit, suppose its radius r exceeds √5. The outer box is [-3,3]^{2}, so its center (x,y) must satisfy |x|,|y|<3-√5<1.
By symmetry take x,y≥0. Then (1-x)^{2}+(2-y)^{2}≤5, so the inward corner (1,2) lies less than r from the center. Such a circle crosses the boundary there, a contradiction. Thus 5π is maximal.
The semicircle's area is πr^{2}/2=2π, giving r^{2}=4 and r=2.
Its center lies on the triangle's hypotenuse, and the circular boundary is tangent to both perpendicular legs.
Therefore the center is 2 units from each leg. In the isosceles right triangle, place the legs on the coordinate axes so the center is (2,2).
The hypotenuse has equal intercepts, and passes through (2,2), so its equation is x+y=4. Both legs consequently have length 4.
The triangle's area is 4×4÷2=8. The circle's radius determines the distances to both legs before the full leg length is found.
The semicircle's center is the midpoint of the triangle's base. Divide the original figure through this midpoint to work with one right-triangle half.
That half has perpendicular legs of lengths 8 and 15, so its area is 8×15/2 = 60. Its hypotenuse has length √(8^{2}+15^{2}) = 17.
The circle is tangent to this sloping side. The radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the side, so the perpendicular distance from the base midpoint to the hypotenuse is r.
Using the hypotenuse as the base of the same half-triangle gives area 17r/2. Equating the two area formulas yields 17r/2 = 60, hence r = 120/17.
The right triangle has legs 5 and 12, so AB = √(5^{2}+12^{2}) = 13 and its area is 5×12/2 = 30.
Let O be the circle's center and r its radius. Since O lies on AC and the circle is tangent to BC, OC = r. Tangency to AB also makes the perpendicular distance from O to AB equal to r.
Segment BO divides triangle ABC into triangles AOB and BOC. Using AB and BC as their respective bases, their areas are 13r/2 and 5r/2.
Therefore 30 = 13r/2+5r/2 = 9r. Dividing by 9 gives r = 10/3. This uses the same radius for both perpendicular distances supplied by the tangencies.
The two lines have equations y=x/3 and y=10-x/2. For 15≤x≤16, the first has y≥5, meeting the rectangle only at (15,5).
Over the same x-range, the second has y≤2.5, below the rectangle's lower edge y=3. Hence there is exactly 1 intersection point.
Use grid coordinates with B=(0,0). The other marked points are F=(6,5), A=(7,3), and C=(2,4).
A shortest horizontal-and-vertical route has length equal to the sum of its horizontal and vertical changes. The four successive legs have lengths 3, 10, 6, and 5, totaling 24.
Use AB and CD as the parallel sides of a trapezoid. Their lengths are 4 and 2, and their perpendicular separation is 6.
The trapezoid area formula is (sum of parallel sides)×height÷2.
Substitution gives (4+2)×6÷2=6×3=18.
The separation of the parallel sides is the height; using a slanted connecting side instead would not give the correct area. The required area is 18 square units.
Find the pairwise intersections of the three boundary lines. They are (-4,5), (4,5), and (0,1).
The first two points lie on the horizontal line y=5, so they form a convenient base of length 4-(-4)=8.
The perpendicular height from (0,1) to this line is 5-1=4. This height measures the distance to the line containing the base, which is the quantity needed in the triangle area formula.
Therefore the triangular region has area (1/2)×8×4=16 square units. Using a horizontal base makes the height a vertical coordinate difference, so no slanted side lengths are needed.
Start in the first grid square. Crossing an internal vertical or horizontal grid line normally enters one additional square.
The segment crosses 2999 internal vertical lines and 4999 internal horizontal lines. Counting these independently would give 1+2999+4999 squares.

At an internal lattice point, however, both lines are crossed simultaneously and only one new square is entered. There are gcd(3000,5000)-1=999 such points, so subtract 999. Those lattice points occur at (3j,5j) for j=1,2,...,999; the two endpoints are excluded because they are not internal crossings.
The result is 1+2999+4999-999=7000. Equivalently, the grid-square formula gives 3000+5000-gcd(3000,5000)=7000.
Number rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right. The unshaded cells (1,1), (1,3), (3,4), and (4,2) have shaded mirror partners.
All four must be shaded. Cell (1,4) lies on the reflection axis and need not change. Thus four additions complete the symmetry.
Combine the rotations using their directions: 3.75 counterclockwise turns minus 2.25 clockwise turns gives a net 1.5 counterclockwise turns.
One complete turn returns to the same direction, so only the remaining half-turn matters. A half-turn from west points east, giving choice B.
Compare the numbers of reflection axes of the five shapes. The equilateral triangle has 3; the nonsquare rhombus has 2; the nonsquare rectangle has 2.
The isosceles trapezoid has 1 axis, while the square has 4. Therefore the square has the greatest number of lines of symmetry.
Reflection across y=x swaps the coordinates: (x,y) becomes (y,x). Reflection of this point across the horizontal axis then gives (y,-x).
This combined rule is a 90° clockwise rotation about the intersection of the axes. Applying it to both the location and orientation of the letter gives diagram E.
Track which edges are folds. The lower-right corner of the final folded square is where the two folded edges meet, so it represents the center of the original paper.
Cutting the small triangular corner and unfolding twice creates four reflected triangles. Together they form a diamond-shaped hole at the center, as in diagram E.
After unfolding, the two end pieces are rectangles measuring 4 by 1. Each has perimeter 2(4+1)=10.
The middle piece is a rectangle measuring 4 by 2, because its two unit-wide parts remain joined at the fold.
Its perimeter is 2(4+2)=12.
The requested ratio is therefore 10:12=5:6, or 5/6. The central piece must be treated as one joined rectangle; adding the perimeters of two separate narrow strips would count an internal edge.
The large square has side length 5. The segment BC is 2 units to the left of side WZ.
Both B and C are 1 unit from the corresponding upper or lower side, so BC=5−1−1=3.
The center O is 2.5 units from WZ, on its other side from BC. Its perpendicular distance from BC is therefore 2+2.5=4.5.
Folding maps O to A while preserving its distance from the fold line BC. Thus triangle ABC has base 3 and height 4.5.
Its area is 3×4.5÷2=6.75=27/4. Reflection across the fold supplies the height directly; the slanted sides of the folded triangle do not need to be calculated.
Let the inner square have side s and make angle θ with the outer frame. By symmetry take 0 ≤ θ ≤ 45°. Set c = cosθ, d = sinθ, and u = c+d. Its horizontal and vertical span is t = su ≤ 5.

Suppose s^{2} > 15. Use coordinates centered on the outer frame and rotate the axes to align with the inner square. The four inward corner vertices occupy the four quadrants, and each coordinate has absolute value at most 1.5u ≤ 7.5/s < s/2.

The square's center can move by at most (5−t)/2 in either original coordinate. In rotated coordinates, each center coordinate therefore has absolute value at most u(5−t)/2 = t(5−t)/(2s) ≤ 25/(8s) < s/2.

Choose an inward corner vertex in the center's quadrant. In each coordinate, the center and vertex have the same sign and both magnitudes are less than s/2. Their coordinate differences are therefore less than s/2, putting that vertex strictly inside the inner square. A small neighborhood then extends into a missing corner, a contradiction. Hence s^{2} ≤ 15.

To attain 15, choose the edge's horizontal and vertical components x,y with x+y = 5 and xy = 5, and center the square. Its vertices touch the frame and its sides pass through the inward corner vertices. Removing the four corner triangles from the 5×5 frame gives area 25−4(xy/2) = 25−10 = 15.
Use the cylinder volume formula V=πr^{2}h. The first cylinder contributes the factor 3^{2}×12=108, and the second contributes 6^{2}×6=216.
The common factor π cancels in the ratio. Hence the volume ratio is 108:216=1:2.
Let s be the edge length of the cube. Its net consists of six square faces, so the given area gives 6s^{2}=18.
Thus s^{2}=3 and s=√3. The volume is s^{3}=s×s^{2}=√3×3=3√3.
The new container has twice the old length, twice the old width, and twice the old height.
Volume is the product of these three dimensions, so its scale factor is 2×2×2=8.
Assuming the same packing of jelly beans, the number of beans scales with volume. Multiply the original estimate by 8: 125×8=1000.
Doubling all dimensions does not merely double the capacity; all three independent length factors contribute. The estimated number is therefore 1000 jelly beans.
Each face of the large cube is divided into a 3 by 3 grid, containing nine equal small squares.
Four corner squares of that face are black. The other 9−4=5 squares are white.
All six faces have the same proportions. The whole surface therefore has white fraction (6×5)/(6×9)=5/9.
Counting by faces is valid for surface area: even at a physical cube corner, differently oriented small faces are separate exposed squares and must each be included.
The solid contains one central unit cube and six outer unit cubes, so its volume is 7 cubic units.
Every face of the central cube is covered by an outer cube. It contributes no exposed surface.
Each outer cube has one face attached to the center and five exposed faces. The exposed area is therefore 6×5=30 square units.
Thus volume to surface-area ratio is 7:30. Counting all seven cubes as separate would incorrectly include the twelve unit faces hidden at the six contacts.
The outside rectangular solid has volume 12×10×5 = 600 cubic units. Find the hollow part separately, then subtract it.
With the stated wall and base thicknesses, the cavity has length 10, width 8, and depth 4. Its volume is 10×8×4 = 320 cubic units.

Therefore the solid material occupies 600−320 = 280 cubic units. Each unit cube contributes one cubic unit, so 280 cubes are required. Subtracting the cavity also counts corners and edges correctly without overlap.
The original cube has side length 2, so its surface area is 6×2^{2}=24 square units.
The attached unit cube contributes six unit faces, but the contact hides one face of the small cube and one unit square of the original cube.
The net increase is therefore 6−2=4 square units. The new exposed area is 24+4=28.
To find the percentage increase, divide by the original surface area, not the new surface area: 4/24=1/6.
Thus the increase is about 16.67%, whose nearest listed percentage is 17%. The contact must be removed from both cubes when counting the visible surface.
Six unit cubes have 6×6=36 faces if counted separately before they are joined.
Whenever two cubes share a full face, that shared contact hides two unit faces: one belonging to each cube.
The diagram contains five such face-to-face contacts. Thus the number of hidden faces is 5×2=10.
Subtract these hidden faces from the separate-cube total: 36−10=26 exposed square units.

Each contact must be counted once as a pair and then multiplied by 2. Subtracting only five would leave one face from every internal contact incorrectly exposed. Edge-only or point-only meetings do not hide any full face and require no subtraction.
Convert the stone's displaced volume into cubic centimeters: it displaces 1000 cubic centimeters of water.
The tank's rectangular base has area 100×40=4000 square centimeters.
If the water level rises by h centimeters, the added volume beneath the new level is base area×rise=4000h.
Equating this with the displaced volume gives 4000h=1000, hence h=1000/4000=0.25 centimeter.

The water does not overflow, so all the displaced volume contributes to the level rise. The stone's own shape is unnecessary; only its volume and the tank's constant horizontal cross-sectional area determine the rise.
The sloping plane passes through the cylinder's center. Central symmetry of the cylinder takes every point in one piece to a point in the other piece.
This transformation preserves volume, so the two pieces have equal volumes. The wedge therefore has half the cylinder's volume.
The cylinder has diameter 8, hence radius 4, and length 6.
Its full volume is π×4^{2}×6=96π, so the wedge volume is 96π/2=48π.

Using π≈3.14 gives 48π≈150.8, nearest to 151 cubic units. The equal-volume conclusion comes from the center symmetry, rather than from the sloping face appearing to divide the drawing into equal areas.
The four block heights are 1/2, 1/3, 1/17, and 11/102. Converting to denominator 102 gives (51+34+6+11)/102 = 1, so their total height is 1.
After the blocks are placed side by side, the horizontal top and bottom faces contribute total area 8. The two long vertical sides contribute 2 times the sum of the heights, or 2.

For the C-B-A-D height profile, the exposed end faces and step faces have total vertical contribution twice the maximum height. This follows by adding the rises and falls of the profile; the intermediate heights cancel.
The maximum height is 1/2, so these remaining faces contribute 2×(1/2) = 1. The full surface area is therefore 8+2+1 = 11.
The cube has side length 10, so its total surface area is 6×10^{2} = 600 square units.
The green portion covers 300 square units. Therefore the total white area is the complement, 600−300 = 300 square units.
Each of the six faces has the same white-square pattern, so these 300 square units are shared equally among six white squares.
Each white square therefore has area 300/6 = 50. There is no need to find its side length, because the question asks for area directly.
A cube has 12 edges, 8 vertices, and 6 faces. These are three different types of features, so count each category separately.
The required total is 12+8+6=26. The answer is E; no geometric measurements or assumptions about the cube's side length are needed.
The bottom layer is the border of a 4 by 3 rectangle. It contains 10 cubes, and the four upper corner cubes bring the total to 14.
A bottom corner cube touches three other cubes, leaving only three faces exposed.
An upper corner cube has five exposed faces.

The remaining six cubes in the bottom layer each touch two neighbors, leaving 6−2=4 exposed faces. Therefore exactly six cubes have four painted faces. Count exposed faces cube by cube rather than using the total surface area.
Each projection occupies three squares, so at least three cubes are needed.
Suppose there were exactly three. The upper cube and two lower cubes would have to use different horizontal and depth positions to reproduce both projections.
The lower cubes would then lie diagonally apart, leaving one cube without the required face connection. Thus three cubes cannot satisfy all conditions.
Four cubes suffice: place three in an L shape on the bottom and one above the corner of the L. Both projections are obtained, so the minimum is four.
A 3×3×3 cube has 27 positions, but only its central position is completely hidden from the surface. Thus at most one of the six white small cubes can expose no face.
The other five white cubes must each expose at least one face, giving at least five visible white unit squares.
This lower bound is attainable by placing those five cubes at the centers of five faces. The whole cube has 6×3^{2} = 54 visible unit squares, so the minimum white fraction is 5/54.
Use the three cube views to identify the faces adjacent to the red face R. Together they show that R touches the four faces B,G,W,P.
Every cube face has exactly four adjacent faces and one opposite face. Thus the only remaining face A must be opposite R.
Oppositeness works in both directions, so the face opposite A is R, the red face. This conclusion follows from adjacency rather than the apparent orientation of any single view.
Track the folded octahedron by labeling its six vertices +X,-X,+Y,-Y,+Z,-Z, with opposite signs denoting opposite vertices.
Start with face 6 at (+X,+Y,+Z). Successive folds place Q at (-X,+Y,+Z), face 5 at (+X,-Y,+Z), face 4 at (+X,-Y,-Z), face 3 at (-X,-Y,-Z), and face 1 at (-X,+Y,-Z).
The right edge of Q joins -X to +Y. Face 1 contains those same two vertices, so face 1 lies across that edge.
Each small cube has two adjacent shaded faces. To hide both faces, the cube must touch other cubes across at least two faces.
With fewer than four cubes, some cube must have fewer than two face-neighbors. In particular, three cubes cannot all touch one another face-to-face, so they cannot form the necessary closed chain.
Four cubes arranged in a 2×2×1 block do work. Each cube has two adjacent inward faces that can be shaded and hidden. Thus the minimum is 4.

Scale the cube edge to 1. The section EJCI is a rhombus, so its area is half the product of its perpendicular diagonals. Indeed, the perpendicular diagonals split a rhombus into four right triangles, whose combined area is half the product of the full diagonals.
Diagonal EC is a body diagonal of the cube, with length √(1^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2})=√3. Diagonal JI is a horizontal face diagonal, with length √(1^{2}+1^{2})=√2.
Therefore the section area is (1/2)√3×√2=√6/2. A cube face has area 1, so the area ratio is R=√6/2.
Squaring gives R^{2}=(√6/2)^{2}=6/4=3/2. Scaling the cube would multiply both areas equally, leaving this ratio unchanged.
Use the dimensions preserved when the net folds into the triangular prism. Its axis length is HJ=EF=8.
In the right-triangular base, BJ=AH=8. The other perpendicular leg is JG=GH-HJ=14-8=6.

Therefore the base area is (1/2)×8×6=24 square units. The factor 1/2 is necessary because the base is triangular, even though the perpendicular edge lengths can be read from rectangular parts of the net.
A prism's volume equals its base area times its axis length. Thus the volume is 24×8=192 cubic units. This uses the two perpendicular base legs, rather than an edge measured across the flattened net.
The smallest prime number is 2. A number divisible by this prime must be even.
Among the listed candidates, only 58 is even, and 58=2×29 shows that it is a product of two primes. Thus the correct choice is C.
Factor 250 completely: 250=2×125=2×5^{3}. Its prime divisors are 2 and 5.
The question asks for distinct prime divisors, so 5 is included once even though its exponent is 3. Their sum is 2+5=7.
The number 1A2 must be divisible by 11. By the divisibility rule, the alternating digit sum 1−A+2 = 3−A must be a multiple of 11.
Since A is a digit from 0 through 9, only A = 3 works. The number is 132 = 11×12.
Factor 2016 into primes: 2016 = 2^{5}×3^{2}×7.
The question asks for distinct prime factors, so count each prime only once rather than adding repeated copies. The sum is 2+3+7 = 12.
Divisibility by 9 requires the digit sum 11+U to be a multiple of 9. Since U is a digit, the only possibility is U=7.
The number is therefore 20187. Divide by 8: 20187=8×2523+3, so the remainder is 3.
Write a two-digit number as 10t+d, where t is its tens digit and d is its nonzero units digit. Divisibility by d is equivalent to d dividing 10t.
For t=1, the valid units digits are 1, 2, 5: three choices. For t=2, they are 1, 2, 4, 5: four choices.
For t=3, they are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6: five choices. For t=4, there are again five choices.
Adding the counts gives 3+4+5+5=17 numbers.
The smallest three-digit multiple of 13 is 13×8=104; the preceding multiple, 91, has only two digits.
The largest is 13×76=988; the next multiple, 1001, has four digits.
Thus the valid multipliers are every integer from 8 through 76.
The count is 76−8+1=69. Include both endpoints; subtracting the multipliers without adding 1 would omit one valid multiple.
The first eight games have total score 37. The ninth score lies from 0 to 9, so the new total lies from 37 to 46.
Its average must be an integer, requiring a total divisible by 9. The only such total is 45, so game nine scores 45−37=8.
After game ten, the total lies from 45 to 54. The only multiple of 10 there is 50, giving tenth score 5.
The product is 8×5=40.
To verify that 67 is prime, test primes no larger than √67, which is less than 9. None of 2, 3, 5, or 7 divides 67.
The distinct prime factors are therefore 2, 3, 5, and 67. Their sum is 2+3+5+67 = 77. Each distinct prime is included only once.
Matching this to the given prime-power form gives w = 2, x = 1, y = 0, and z = 2. The exponent of 5 is zero because 5 does not divide 588.
Substitute into the requested expression: 2w+3x+5y+7z = 2×2+3×1+5×0+7×2 = 4+3+0+14 = 21.
The two smallest allowed prime factors are 53 and 59. A product using exactly two prime factors is smallest at 53×53, but that is a perfect square and is excluded.
The next candidate is 53×59 = 3127. It uses allowed primes and is not a square because its two prime factors are distinct.

A number with three or more prime factors would be at least 53^{3}, which already exceeds 3127. Thus neither using more factors nor choosing larger primes can improve the candidate, and the minimum is 3127.
Write four consecutive odd integers as 2k+1, 2k+3, 2k+5, and 2k+7. Their sum is 8k+16 = 8(k+2), always divisible by 8.
Conversely, the equation 8k+16 = S gives the integer k = S/8−2 whenever S is a multiple of 8.
Among the listed values, 16, 40, 72, and 200 are multiples of 8, whereas 100 is not. Therefore 100 cannot be expressed in the required form.
Factor the difference of fourth powers twice: 13^{4}−11^{4} = (13−11)(13+11)(13^{2}+11^{2}).
The factors are 2, 24, and 290. Write 24 = 2^{3}×3 and 290 = 2×145 to separate all powers of 2.
The expression is therefore 2^{5}×435 = 32×435. Since 435 is odd, no additional factor of 2 is available. The greatest power of 2 dividing the expression is exactly 32.

A trailing zero requires a factor 10 = 2×5. There are more factors of 2 than factors of 5, so count the factors of 5. In 98!, multiples of 5 contribute 19 factors and multiples of 25 contribute 3 additional factors.
Thus 98! contains 19+3 = 22 factors of 5. Since 10,000 = 10^{4} contributes four more, the final product has 22+4 = 26 trailing zeros.
Write the alternating five-digit number as ababa. Divisibility by 5 makes its last digit 0 or 5. Since that digit is also the nonzero leading digit a, it must be a=5.
The digit sum is 5+b+5+b+5=15+2b. Divisibility by 3 requires b to be a multiple of 3.
Thus b=0,3,6,9. Each choice produces a valid alternating number, giving 4 possibilities.
There are four choices for the thousands digit and five choices for each other digit, giving 4×5^{3} possible numbers.
Divisibility by 4 depends only on the last two digits. The tens digit t is even, so 10t is divisible by 4. Thus the units digit must be divisible by 4 as well.
The permitted units digits are 0, 4, and 8: three of the five choices. The favorable count is 4×5×5×3, so the fraction is 3/5.
Call the common front-plus-back sum S. Suppose S were even.
The backs of the even front numbers 44 and 38 would both have to be even primes. The only even prime is 2, so this would repeat a number, violating distinctness.
Hence S is odd. The back of the odd number 59 must then be the even prime 2, giving S=59+2=61.
The other back numbers are 61−44=17 and 61−38=23, which are distinct primes.
Their average is (2+17+23)/3=42/3=14. Parity forces the common sum before any search over possible prime triples is needed.
The condition that n/3 has three digits gives 100≤n/3≤999, hence 300≤n≤2997.
The condition that 3n has three digits gives 100≤3n≤999. In particular, n≤333.
Combining the two ranges yields 300≤n≤333.
Also n/3 must be an integer, so n is divisible by 3. The candidates are 300, 303, 306, and so on through 333.

This arithmetic sequence has (333−300)/3+1=12 terms. The added 1 includes both endpoints. Each listed n makes both n/3 and 3n three-digit integers, so the combined conditions are sufficient as well as necessary.
Use the digit-sum test for divisibility by 3. The two numbers have digit sums 19+A+B and 15+A+B+C.
Both digit sums are multiples of 3, so their difference must also be a multiple of 3. Subtracting cancels A and B and gives C−4.
Thus C−4 is divisible by 3, or C has remainder 1 on division by 3. The possible digit remainders are enough to answer the question; there is no need to solve for A and B.
Among the listed choices for C, only 1 has the required remainder. Therefore C = 1 is the requested choice.
Count factors of 7 in 1!×2!×...×51!. A multiple 7k appears in every factorial from (7k)! through 51!, so it appears 52-7k times.
For k=1 through 7, these contributions are 45, 38, 31, 24, 17, 10, and 3. Their sum is 168.
This counts one factor of 7 from every multiple of 7. However, 49=7^{2} contains a second factor of 7.

That extra factor appears in 49!, 50!, and 51!, adding 3. Hence the total exponent is 168+3=171. There is no further correction for 7^{3}, since 343 exceeds 51. Thus all possible powers of 7 have now been included.
Prime factorization gives 180 = 2^{2}×3^{2}×5 and 594 = 2×3^{3}×11. Their greatest common divisor is 2×3^{2} = 18.
Their least common multiple is 2^{2}×3^{3}×5×11 = 5,940. The requested ratio is 5,940/18 = 330.
A number divisible by 15, 20, and 25 must be a multiple of their least common multiple.
Using prime factors, 15=3×5, 20=2^{2}×5, and 25=5^{2}, so the least common multiple is 2^{2}×3×5^{2}=300.
The multiples of 300 between 1000 and 2000 are 1200, 1500, and 1800.
The neighboring multiples 900 and 2100 lie outside the interval. Therefore exactly three numbers qualify, giving choice C.
Let k be the common number of boys and girls who pass. The given passing fractions imply a total of 3k/2 boys and 4k/3 girls.
Both totals must be integers. Thus k is divisible by both 2 and 3, so the least possible positive k is 6.
This gives 3×6/2=9 boys and 4×6/3=8 girls.
The minimum total is 9+8=17 students. Larger allowed k values are multiples of 6 and increase both group sizes proportionally.
The common unit price in cents must divide both 143 and 195. Factor them as 143 = 11×13 and 195 = 3×5×13.
Their common positive divisors are 1 and 13. A 1-cent price would require 143 sixth graders, exceeding the limit of 30, so the price must be 13 cents.
The two class counts are then 143/13 = 11 and 195/13 = 15. Their difference is 15−11 = 4 students.
The common unit price, measured in cents, must divide both purchase totals. Factor them: 143 = 11×13 and 187 = 11×17.
Their greatest common divisor is 11, so the only possible common prices are 1 cent and 11 cents. The condition that the price exceeds 1 cent forces a price of 11 cents.
The purchase quantities differ by (187−143)/11 = 44/11 = 4. Equivalently, the quantities are 17 and 13, whose difference is 4.
The eighth-grade count must be divisible by both 5 and 8. Its smallest possible positive value is lcm(5,8) = 40.
Using the stated grade ratios with 40 eighth graders gives 24 sixth graders and 25 seventh graders.

Thus the minimum combined enrollment is 40+24+25 = 89. Any larger admissible eighth-grade count scales the other grade counts by the same factor, so it cannot produce a smaller total. The minimum therefore occurs at 40.
The conditions imply that b divides both 12 and 15. Thus b is a divisor of gcd(12,15) = 3, so b is 1 or 3.
Neither possibility supplies a factor of 4 or 5. Consequently a must contain the factor 4 required by 12, and c must contain the factor 5 required by 15.
It follows that lcm(a,c) is divisible by both 4 and 5, hence is at least 20. The choice a = 4, b = 3, c = 5 satisfies the conditions and gives lcm(a,c) = 20, attaining this bound.
List the positive factor pairs of 24: (1,24), (2,12), (3,8), and (4,6). Each pair has the required product.
Their sums are 25, 14, 11, and 10 respectively. Only 3 and 8 have sum 11, so the larger number is 8.
For positive integers w and l satisfying wl=12, list the possible pairs: (1,12), (2,6), (3,4), (4,3), (6,2), (12,1).
The points decrease as w increases, but do not lie on a straight line. Only graph A shows this set of integer points.
Evaluate the nested boxes from the inside outward. The inner input is 11, whose positive divisors are 1 and 11, summing to 12.
The positive divisor pairs of 12 are (1,12), (2,6), and (3,4). Their total is 1+12+2+6+3+4=28.
A positive integer is a perfect square exactly when every prime factor has an even exponent. The number 1 is also a square.
Both 3^{2018} and 5^{2020} have even exponents, while 4^{2019} = (2^{2019})^{2}. But 2^{2017} has an odd prime exponent, so it is the only nonsquare.
The sum of the integers from 1 through 9 is 45. Omitting one of those numbers leaves a total between 45-9=36 and 45-1=44.
The only perfect square in this interval is 36. Thus the omitted number is 45-36=9.
Factor the starting number: 360 = 2^{3}×3^{2}×5. To make a perfect square, every prime exponent must become even.
The smallest required multiplier is therefore x = 2×5 = 10, raising the exponents of 2 and 5 to 4 and 2.

To make a perfect cube, every exponent must instead be a multiple of 3. The exponent of 2 is already suitable; the others need one factor of 3 and two factors of 5. Thus y = 3×5^{2} = 75, and x+y = 85.
Factor the number completely: 23232=2^{6}×3×11^{2}. Every positive divisor is determined by choosing an exponent for each prime.
The exponent of 2 can be 0 through 6, giving 7 choices. The exponent of 3 can be 0 or 1, giving 2 choices. The exponent of 11 can be 0,1,2, giving 3 choices.
These choices are independent, so the number of positive divisors is 7×2×3=42.
Factor 2020=2^{2}×5×101. A positive divisor chooses exponents 0,1,2 for 2 and 0,1 for each of the other primes. Thus there are 3×2×2=12 divisors.
Exclude divisors having at most three positive divisors themselves. These are 1; the primes 2,5,101; and the prime square 4.
These five cases are the only exclusions: other divisors have at least four divisors. Hence the required count is 12-5=7.
An arrangement in equal rows corresponds to choosing a positive divisor as the number of people per row. Therefore the desired total must have exactly 12 positive divisors.
It must also be a multiple of 30. Test the smallest positive multiples in order: 30, 60, and so on.
Since 30 = 2×3×5, it has (1+1)(1+1)(1+1) = 8 positive divisors, so it fails. But 60 = 2^{2}×3×5 has (2+1)(1+1)(1+1) = 12 divisors.
There is no positive multiple of 30 strictly between 30 and 60. Consequently 60 is the smallest possible total satisfying both requirements.
Count the perfect cubes by counting their integer cube roots. At the lower endpoint, 2^{8}+1=257 lies between 6^{3}=216 and 7^{3}=343. Thus the smallest allowable cube root is 7.

At the upper endpoint, 2^{18}+1=262145=64^{3}+1. Therefore 64^{3} is included, but 65^{3} is already too large. This checks both endpoints directly: the final permitted cube is just one unit below the upper bound, while the next cube lies above it.
Every integer cube root from 7 through 64 gives exactly one admissible perfect cube, and the function n^{3} is strictly increasing for positive integers.
The number of these integers is 64-7+1=58.
Write N+1=k^{2}. Because this square ends in 00, k is a multiple of 10. Since N has four digits, k can be 40,50,60,70,80,90,100.
Factor N=k^{2}-1=(k-1)(k+1). Both factors exceed 1, so for N to be a product of two primes, each factor must itself be prime.
Only (59,61) consists of two primes. It gives N=59×61=3599. This is a four-digit number whose successor is 60^{2}, so there is exactly 1 valid N.
Divide 23 by 6: 23 = 3×6+5. Five cars fill the incomplete group, so it needs one additional car.
Adding one gives 24 = 4×6, which divides evenly into six equal groups. Therefore the smallest possible addition is 1 car.
A two-digit number ending in 3 must be one of 13, 23, 33, ..., 93. Among these, only 73 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9.
Now divide 73 by 11: 73 = 6×11+7. Its remainder is therefore 7.
Only the units digit affects the units digit of the result. Each relevant power ends in 2, so the units calculation is 2-2-2-2-2-2=-8.
Adding 10 gives the equivalent nonnegative remainder 2. Therefore the original integer has units digit 2.
The five numbers sum to 15+16+17+18+19=85. To make the remaining sum divisible by 4, remove a number with the same remainder as 85.
Since 85 leaves remainder 1, remove 17, the only listed number congruent to 1 modulo 4. The remaining sum is 68.
The units digits of successive powers of 9 alternate: 9, 1, 9, 1, and so on. Every odd exponent therefore produces units digit 9.
Both exponents in the expression are odd, so each term ends in 9.
For the units digit of a sum, only the units digits of the terms matter. Thus add 9+9=18.
The sum has units digit 8. Higher place values and the sizes of the exponents do not affect this conclusion.
Let the required number be N. The remainder condition says N−2 is a positive multiple of 3, 4, 5, and 6.
